claim: Leonardo of Pisa's Liber abaci is dated 1202 in its opening line, and its first chapter begins: 'The nine figures of the Indians are these: 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1'.

evidence.quote: Incipit liber Abaci Compositus a leonardo filio Bonaci j Pisano
evidence.translation: Here begins the Book of the Abacus composed by Leonardo son of Bonacci, Pisan, in the year 1202 (next line: 'In Anno. M * cc* ij.°')

evidence.locator: p.2, Incipit primum capitulum (OCR line 197-198; OCR reads 'imiorum be' for 'indorum hee')
evidence.quote: Nouem figure imiorum be sunt
evidence.translation: The nine figures of the Indians are these

notes: OCR misreads 'indorum' here; the chapter list on the same page reads 'De cognitione uouem figurarum yndorum'. 'Fibonacci' is a later nickname: the text says 'Leonardo son of Bonacci'.

claim: Leonardo adds a tenth sign, 0, 'which in Arabic is called zephirum': in his book the Arabic link is the name of zero, while the nine figures are called Indian.

evidence.quote: quod arahicc zephirum appellatur
evidence.translation: which is called zephirum in Arabic (full: 'With these nine figures, and with this sign 0 ... any number is written')

notes: Do not extend to 'zephirum became zero/cipher': etymology not in our sources.

claim: Leonardo writes that his father, a public scribe at a customs house for Pisan merchants, brought him there as a boy to study the abacus, where he was introduced to the art 'through the nine figures of the Indians'.

evidence.quote: publicus scriba in duana hugee pro pisanis mercatoribus
evidence.translation: a public scribe in the customs house of [Bugia] for the Pisan merchants

evidence.quote: in arte per noucm figuras indorum intro-
evidence.translation: introduced to the art through the nine figures of the Indians

notes: OCR reads 'hugee'; the usual reading is 'bugee' (Bugia = Béjaïa, Algeria) but that identification is NOT verified in our sources (C012). Say 'a customs house where his father worked' unless G6 confirms.

claim: The Latin al-Khwarizmi text (Cambridge University Library MS Ii.6.5) opens 'Dixit algoritmi' and sets out to explain 'the numbering of the Indians by nine letters'.

evidence.quote: Dixit algoritmi: laudes deo rectori nostro
evidence.translation: Algoritmi said: praise to God our ruler

evidence.quote: tefacere de numero indorum per .ix. litcras
evidence.translation: to set out the numbering of the Indians by nine letters

evidence.quote: Dixit algoritmi: Cum uidissem yndos constituisse .ix. litcras
evidence.translation: Algoritmi said: when I had seen that the Indians had set up nine letters

notes: Our source does not date the Latin version, does not name Baghdad and does not give al-Khwarizmi's dates. The title 'Algoritmi de numero Indorum' is the 1857 editor's heading.

claim: The same text says the Indians worked with places (units, tens, hundreds) and put 'a little circle like the letter o' in a place to show it was empty.

evidence.quote: Et inueni quod operati sunt yndi ex his differentiis
evidence.translation: And I found that the Indians worked with these places

evidence.quote: circulum paruulum in simi-
evidence.translation: [they placed in it] a little circle in the likeness of the letter o, so they would know the units place was empty

notes: Place value and a placeholder circle, both credited to the Indians. It does not say who first used zero as a number. Gate WARN is a checker artefact: a stray OCR "<" at line 72 makes the tag-stripper delete lines 72-458 of the copy; both quotes are at OCR lines 119 and 141 verbatim.

claim: The Bodleian's 2017 radiocarbon test found the Bakhshali manuscript, which uses a dot for zero hundreds of times, dates 'from as early as the 3rd or 4th century'; its 70 birch-bark leaves come from at least three different periods.

evidence.quote: it dates from as early as the 3rd or 4th century
a seminal mathematical text which contains hundreds of zeroes
consists of 70 fragile leaves of birch bark, is in fact composed of material from at least three different periods
The zero symbol that we use today evolved from a dot that was used in ancient India and can be seen throughout the Bakhshali manuscript

notes: Holder's statement; the release does not say which leaves carry which date. Keep 'as early as' and 'some leaves'. Earlier scholarly dating (Hayashi) was 8th-12th century: see conflicts K1.

claim: The Bakhshali manuscript was found in 1881 in a field at the village of Bakhshali, near Peshawar, in today's Pakistan; it has been at Oxford's Bodleian Library since 1902.

evidence.quote: The Bakhshali manuscript was found in 1881, buried in a field in a village called Bakhshali, near Peshawar, in what is now a region of Pakistan
presented it to the Bodleian Library in 1902, where it has been kept since

notes: 'Indian' in the sources means the subcontinent; the find spot is in Pakistan today.

claim: Our measurement: Leonardo's 1202 book came about 800 to 1,000 years after the earliest Bakhshali leaves (3rd-4th century) and 574 years after Brahmagupta's 628 text.

evidence.quote: In Anno. M * cc* ij.°
it dates from as early as the 3rd or 4th century
this happened in 628 AD

method: method/numerals_measure.py section 'Time gaps' -> method/numerals_measure_output.txt (201..400 to 1202 = 1,001..802 years; 628 to 1202 = 574)

claim: According to the Bodleian, placeholder zeros were also used by the Babylonians and Maya; zero as a number in its own right first appears in Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 AD); a 9th-century Gwalior temple inscription was earlier thought the oldest Indian placeholder zero.

evidence.quote: the use of zero as a placeholder was seen in several different ancient cultures, such as among the ancient Mayans and Babylonians
which is the first document to discuss zero as a number
predates a 9th-century inscription of zero on the wall of a temple in Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh

notes: Bodleian is not the holder of Brahmagupta's text or the Gwalior inscription; attribute ('the Bodleian says').

claim: Leonardo ranks the 'algorismus' and the 'arcs of Pythagoras' as almost an error compared with 'the method of the Indians'.

evidence.quote: gorc quasi errorem computaui respectu modi indorum
evidence.translation: I counted [them] almost an error compared with the method of the Indians

notes: Fresh angle: by 1202 'algorismus' was a rival method's name in his own book.
